items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The Digital Society internal assessment, in which students investigate a real-world digital system and its impacts on people and communities"?
options: inquiry focus
perspective
digital system
inquiry project
items.answer: inquiry project
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of inquiry project.

items.stem: Explain why a narrow inquiry focus leads to a stronger inquiry.
items.answer: A specific system, stakeholder group and context allow in-depth research and analysis within the time and length limits, whereas a broad topic leads to general description.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A specific system, stakeholder group and context allow in-depth research and analysis within the time and length limits, whereas a broad topic leads to general description. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Any interesting technology is a suitable inquiry focus." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The focus must be a real-world digital system with identifiable impacts on people or communities that can be researched.
items.markingKey: The focus must be a real-world digital system with identifiable impacts on people or communities that can be researched. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Students should select a digital system that is real and that has impacts on people and communities."
— Paraphrase of IB Digital Society internal assessment guidance

Explain how a student could check that their chosen system meets this requirement.
items.answer: Identify the system's components and stakeholders, find evidence of actual effects on people, and confirm there are sources describing these impacts.
items.markingKey: Identify the system's components and stakeholders, find evidence of actual effects on people, and confirm there are sources describing these impacts. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to refining an inquiry focus, explain how it illustrates formulating an inquiry focus.
items.answer: A student starts with "AI in education", narrows to "generative-AI tools in my school", and finally to "the impacts of a generative-AI tutoring tool on students' independent learning at my school". Narrowing to a specific system, group and impact makes the inquiry manageable.
items.markingKey: Context (A student starts with "AI in education", narrows to "generative-AI tools in my school", and finally to "the impacts of a generative-AI tutoring tool on students' independent learning at my school".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: narrowing to a specific system, group and impact makes the inquiry manageable. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to formulating an inquiry focus.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A local digital system is a better choice for the inquiry than a global one."
items.answer: A global system examined in a local context often combines the advantages of both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access to primary evidence; personal relevance and engagement. Arguments against: fewer published sources; global systems have broader implications. Supported judgement: A global system examined in a local context often combines the advantages of both.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "guiding question"?
options: A question that directs the research, such as "How has a food-delivery app affected the working conditions of riders in my city?"
The effects of the digital system on people and communities that the presentation analyses
Original evidence collected or produced first-hand, such as interviews, surveys, company policies or laws
Images, charts, screenshots or short clips that support claims in the presentation, with sources acknowledged
items.answer: A question that directs the research, such as "How has a food-delivery app affected the working conditions of riders in my city?"
items.markingKey: A. "guiding question" is a question that directs the research, such as "How has a food-delivery app affected the working conditions of riders in my city?".

items.stem: Evaluate two possible inquiry foci and justify which is more suitable.
items.answer: Specificity; real system; impacts on people; available sources; manageability; justified choice.
items.markingKey: Specificity; real system; impacts on people; available sources; manageability; justified choice.

items.stem: Which is a primary source for an inquiry into a school learning app?
options: An interview with teachers who use the app
A Wikipedia page about the app
A textbook chapter on edtech
A news article summarising education apps
items.answer: An interview with teachers who use the app
items.markingKey: A. Interviews are first-hand evidence.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Academic sources never need evaluating." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Academic studies can be outdated, narrow in sample or funded by interested parties, so they also need evaluation.
items.markingKey: Academic studies can be outdated, narrow in sample or funded by interested parties, so they also need evaluation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why an inquiry should include sources with different perspectives.
items.answer: Different stakeholders experience a system differently; including users, companies, critics and regulators gives a balanced understanding and supports evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different stakeholders experience a system differently; including users, companies, critics and regulators gives a balanced understanding and supports evaluation. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe ethical interviews for an inquiry and explain what it reveals about ethical primary research.
items.answer: A student interviewing classmates about a monitoring app gets informed consent, anonymises responses and stores notes securely. Ethical research protects participants and strengthens the credibility of the inquiry.
items.markingKey: Context (A student interviewing classmates about a monitoring app gets informed consent, anonymises responses and stores notes securely.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: ethical research protects participants and strengthens the credibility of the inquiry. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ethical primary research.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Many students said the app made them feel watched."
— Student interview notes from an inquiry project

Explain one value and one limitation of this source.
items.answer: Value: first-hand perspective of affected users. Limitation: small, possibly unrepresentative sample; responses may be influenced by the interviewer.
items.markingKey: Value: first-hand perspective of affected users. Limitation: small, possibly unrepresentative sample; responses may be influenced by the interviewer. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: For their inquiry, a student sends a questionnaire to 80 students; 48 reply. Of these, 37 say they trust AI chatbots for homework answers. Calculate the response rate and the percentage of respondents who trust AI chatbots for homework answers. Explain one limitation of this evidence and how the student could address it.
items.answer: response rate 60%; 77.1% of respondents; small, self-selected sample may not be representative; corroborate with interviews, published studies or wider data, and acknowledge the limitation
items.markingKey: 48 ÷ 80 × 100 = 60% [M1 A1]; 37 ÷ 48 × 100 = 77.1% [A1]. Representativeness/self-selection/self-report [R1]; triangulation or acknowledgement [R1].

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Primary sources are more valuable than secondary sources for the inquiry project."
items.answer: Combining primary and secondary sources gives the most balanced and reliable inquiry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: first-hand perspectives of affected people; local, specific evidence. Arguments against: small samples; secondary sources give context, scale and expert analysis. Supported judgement: Combining primary and secondary sources gives the most balanced and reliable inquiry.

items.stem: Evaluate three sources a student could use for an inquiry into a digital system, considering claims and perspectives.
items.answer: Identify sources of different types; claims; origin and purpose; value and limitation; how they combine.
items.markingKey: Identify sources of different types; claims; origin and purpose; value and limitation; how they combine.

items.stem: Briefly explain why primary research by students should be conducted ethically.
items.answer: Participants' consent, privacy and anonymity must be protected, especially when collecting personal data from peers or minors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Participants' consent, privacy and anonymity must be protected, especially when collecting personal data from peers or minors. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: For their inquiry, a student sends a questionnaire to 80 students; 60 reply. Of these, 29 say they have changed privacy settings on their phone. Calculate the response rate and the percentage of respondents who have changed privacy settings on their phone.
items.answer: response rate 75%; 48.3% of respondents

items.stem: Which is the best use of visuals in the presentation?
items.answer: Charts and images that support specific claims, with sources cited
items.markingKey: Charts and images that support specific claims, with sources cited. Visuals should communicate evidence.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the presentation should analyse impacts on more than one stakeholder.
items.answer: Different groups experience a system differently, so comparing impacts gives balance and supports a stronger evaluation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different groups experience a system differently, so comparing impacts gives balance and supports a stronger evaluation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The presentation can exceed the time limit if the content is good." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The time limit must be respected; planning and editing are part of the task.
items.markingKey: The time limit must be respected; planning and editing are part of the task. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Visuals should support, not replace, the analysis."
— Paraphrase of common advice on multimedia presentations

Explain how a student could apply this advice.
items.answer: Use each chart or image to illustrate a specific claim and explain what it shows, rather than relying on visuals without commentary.
items.markingKey: Use each chart or image to illustrate a specific claim and explain what it shows, rather than relying on visuals without commentary. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student plans a 10-minute inquiry presentation with sections: the digital system and focus (15%), evidence from sources (25%), impacts and implications for stakeholders (45%), conclusion and further inquiry (15%). Calculate the time for each section in minutes and seconds. Explain why the analysis section is given the most time.
items.answer: the digital system and focus: 1 min 30 s; evidence from sources: 2 min 30 s; impacts and implications for stakeholders: 4 min 30 s; conclusion and further inquiry: 1 min 30 s; analysis and evaluation of impacts and implications is the core of the inquiry and carries the most weight in assessment
items.markingKey: 15% × 10 = 1.5 min = 1 min 30 s; 25% × 10 = 2.5 min = 2 min 30 s; 45% × 10 = 4.5 min = 4 min 30 s; 15% × 10 = 1.5 min = 1 min 30 s [M1 A2]. Analysis of impacts/implications is central to the task [R1 R1].

items.stem: Using a presentation on a school monitoring app as an example, explain analysing impacts and implications.
items.answer: A student analyses a school laptop-monitoring app: impacts on safety, privacy and trust for students, teachers and parents; implications for surveillance norms; conclusion on proportionality. Considering several stakeholders produces a balanced conclusion.
items.markingKey: Context (A student analyses a school laptop-monitoring app: impacts on safety, privacy and trust for students, teachers and parents; implications for surveillance norms; conclusion on proportionality.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: considering several stakeholders produces a balanced conclusion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to analysing impacts and implications.

items.stem: Plan the analysis section of a presentation on a digital system of your choice, evaluating its impacts and implications for two stakeholders.
items.answer: Named system; two stakeholders; impacts; implications; evidence; concept; judgement.
items.markingKey: Named system; two stakeholders; impacts; implications; evidence; concept; judgement.

items.stem: "A recorded multimedia presentation is an effective way to assess a Digital Society inquiry." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: It is effective when assessment focuses on analysis rather than production quality.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: develops digital communication skills; allows evidence to be shown visually. Arguments against: technical skills may affect quality; time limit restricts depth. Supported judgement: It is effective when assessment focuses on analysis rather than production quality. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Briefly explain why sources should be acknowledged in the presentation.
items.answer: Acknowledging sources shows academic honesty, lets the audience judge evidence and distinguishes the student's analysis from others' claims.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Acknowledging sources shows academic honesty, lets the audience judge evidence and distinguishes the student's analysis from others' claims. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student plans a 10-minute inquiry presentation with sections: introduction and inquiry focus (10%), claims and perspectives (30%), analysis of impacts and implications (45%), conclusion (15%). Calculate the time for each section in minutes and seconds.
items.answer: introduction and inquiry focus: 1 min 0 s; claims and perspectives: 3 min 0 s; analysis of impacts and implications: 4 min 30 s; conclusion: 1 min 30 s

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Honesty in academic work, including acknowledging the ideas, words and images of others and declaring the use of AI tools"?
options: claim
primary source
academic integrity
inquiry process document
items.answer: academic integrity
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of academic integrity.

items.stem: A student claims: "Only direct quotations need to be cited." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Paraphrased ideas, data, images and AI-generated content must also be acknowledged.
items.markingKey: Paraphrased ideas, data, images and AI-generated content must also be acknowledged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a reference and a citation.
items.answer: A citation is a brief in-text or on-slide acknowledgement; a reference is the full source details in the reference list.
items.markingKey: A citation is a brief in-text or on-slide acknowledgement; a reference is the full source details in the reference list. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using citing an AI tool as an example, explain academic integrity.
items.answer: A student who used a chatbot to brainstorm search terms states this in the process document and cites the tool and date, as IB guidance requires. Transparent acknowledgement maintains integrity.
items.markingKey: Context (A student who used a chatbot to brainstorm search terms states this in the process document and cites the tool and date, as IB guidance requires.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: transparent acknowledgement maintains integrity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to academic integrity.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Students must acknowledge all sources, including AI tools, used in their work."
— Paraphrase of IB academic integrity policy guidance (2023)

Explain why this requirement is important in the inquiry project.
items.answer: It ensures assessment reflects the student's own work and lets examiners see how sources and tools contributed.
items.markingKey: It ensures assessment reflects the student's own work and lets examiners see how sources and tools contributed. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A 300-word limit is sufficient to document the inquiry process."
items.answer: The limit is sufficient if students prioritise key decisions and reasons.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: forces concise, focused reflection; reduces repetition. Arguments against: complex inquiries may be hard to summarise; little space for detail. Supported judgement: The limit is sufficient if students prioritise key decisions and reasons.

items.stem: Explain why consistent citations are required.
items.answer: They give credit, avoid plagiarism and allow readers to check claims, supporting academic integrity and credibility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They give credit, avoid plagiarism and allow readers to check claims, supporting academic integrity and credibility. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A source that interprets or analyses primary evidence, such as a news article or academic review"?
options: inquiry focus
secondary source
reference list
implications
items.answer: secondary source
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of secondary source.

items.stem: What should the conclusion of the presentation include?
options: A list of all sources
A judgement about impacts and implications that follows from the analysis
A new topic
Only a thank-you slide
items.answer: A judgement about impacts and implications that follows from the analysis
items.markingKey: B. The conclusion answers the inquiry focus.

items.stem: Which inquiry focus is best?
options: "The internet"
"Technology"
"Social media is bad"
"The impacts of a city's e-scooter rental app on pedestrians with disabilities"
items.answer: "The impacts of a city's e-scooter rental app on pedestrians with disabilities"
items.markingKey: D. A good focus names a specific system and specific people affected.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The process document should report the findings of the inquiry.
Reason (R): The process document explains how the inquiry developed.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false; R is true and explains why.

items.stem: Distinguish between limitation of a source and value of a source.
items.answer: Value is what makes the source useful (expertise, first-hand access); limitation is what restricts its usefulness (bias, small sample, age).
items.markingKey: Value is what makes the source useful (expertise, first-hand access); limitation is what restricts its usefulness (bias, small sample, age). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a conclusion and a summary.
items.answer: A summary repeats points; a conclusion makes a judgement that answers the inquiry focus and may suggest further inquiry.
items.markingKey: A summary repeats points; a conclusion makes a judgement that answers the inquiry focus and may suggest further inquiry. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The inquiry project should explain only how a system works technically.
Reason (R): The inquiry analyses impacts on people and communities.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false; R is true and explains why.

items.stem: Explain the difference between description of the process and reflection.
items.answer: Description lists steps taken; reflection evaluates why choices were made and what was learned or changed.
items.markingKey: Description lists steps taken; reflection evaluates why choices were made and what was learned or changed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Academic sources never need evaluating." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Academic studies can be outdated, narrow in sample or funded by interested parties, so they also need evaluation.
items.markingKey: Academic studies can be outdated, narrow in sample or funded by interested parties, so they also need evaluation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Priya writes: "More slides make a better presentation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Clarity, focus and well-chosen evidence matter more than the number of slides.
items.markingKey: Clarity, focus and well-chosen evidence matter more than the number of slides. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe refining an inquiry focus and explain what it reveals about formulating an inquiry focus.
items.answer: A student starts with "AI in education", narrows to "generative-AI tools in my school", and finally to "the impacts of a generative-AI tutoring tool on students' independent learning at my school". Narrowing to a specific system, group and impact makes the inquiry manageable.
items.markingKey: Context (A student starts with "AI in education", narrows to "generative-AI tools in my school", and finally to "the impacts of a generative-AI tutoring tool on students' independent learning at my school".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: narrowing to a specific system, group and impact makes the inquiry manageable. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to formulating an inquiry focus.

items.stem: The inquiry process document has a 300-word limit. A student writes 104 words on inquiry focus and its development and 63 words on selection of sources. Calculate how many words remain for reflection on the process, and the percentage of the limit already used.
items.answer: 133 words; 55.7% used

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our app has increased student engagement by 40%."
— Marketing page of an educational-technology company

Evaluate the value and limitation of this source for an inquiry.
items.answer: Value: shows the company's claims and perspective. Limitation: promotional purpose; the 40% figure lacks method, sample and definition of "engagement", so needs corroboration.
items.markingKey: Value: shows the company's claims and perspective. Limitation: promotional purpose; the 40% figure lacks method, sample and definition of "engagement", so needs corroboration. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe a presentation on a city bike-share app and explain what it reveals about inclusion and access.
items.answer: A student shows usage data and interviews, analysing benefits for commuters and the environment and barriers for people without smartphones or bank cards. Using local data and voices makes the analysis specific and credible.
items.markingKey: Context (A student shows usage data and interviews, analysing benefits for commuters and the environment and barriers for people without smartphones or bank cards.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: using local data and voices makes the analysis specific and credible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to inclusion and access.

items.stem: A student claims: "Any interesting technology is a suitable inquiry focus." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The focus must be a real-world digital system with identifiable impacts on people or communities that can be researched.
items.markingKey: The focus must be a real-world digital system with identifiable impacts on people or communities that can be researched. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The inquiry process document has a 300-word limit. A student writes 115 words on choosing the system and 102 words on research and evaluation of sources. Calculate how many words remain for reflection and changes made, and the percentage of the limit already used.
items.answer: 83 words; 72.3% used

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Primary sources are more valuable than secondary sources for the inquiry project."
items.answer: Combining primary and secondary sources gives the most balanced and reliable inquiry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: first-hand perspectives of affected people; local, specific evidence. Arguments against: small samples; secondary sources give context, scale and expert analysis. Supported judgement: Combining primary and secondary sources gives the most balanced and reliable inquiry.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A recorded multimedia presentation is an effective way to assess a Digital Society inquiry."
items.answer: It is effective when assessment focuses on analysis rather than production quality.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: develops digital communication skills; allows evidence to be shown visually. Arguments against: technical skills may affect quality; time limit restricts depth. Supported judgement: It is effective when assessment focuses on analysis rather than production quality. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: "A local digital system is a better choice for the inquiry than a global one." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: A global system examined in a local context often combines the advantages of both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access to primary evidence; personal relevance and engagement. Arguments against: fewer published sources; global systems have broader implications. Supported judgement: A global system examined in a local context often combines the advantages of both. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "A 300-word limit is sufficient to document the inquiry process." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: The limit is sufficient if students prioritise key decisions and reasons.

Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "triangulation"?
options: A question that directs the research, such as "How has a food-delivery app affected the working conditions of riders in my city?"
Checking a claim using several independent sources or methods
The effects of the digital system on people and communities that the presentation analyses
A source that interprets or analyses primary evidence, such as a news article or academic review
items.answer: Checking a claim using several independent sources or methods
items.markingKey: B. "triangulation" is checking a claim using several independent sources or methods.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "further inquiry"?
options: Questions or directions for future investigation identified in the conclusion
The wider or longer-term consequences of the impacts, such as effects on rights, equality or trust
A clear, specific statement of the digital system and the impacts on people or communities that the inquiry will investigate
The limits of an inquiry – which system, which stakeholders, which place and time – that keep it manageable
items.answer: Questions or directions for future investigation identified in the conclusion
items.markingKey: A. "further inquiry" is questions or directions for future investigation identified in the conclusion.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "scope".
items.answer: The limits of an inquiry – which system, which stakeholders, which place and time – that keep it manageable
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the limits of an inquiry – which system, which stakeholders, which place and time – that keep it manageable. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the process document should explain changes to the inquiry focus.
items.answer: It shows the inquiry developed in response to evidence, demonstrating genuine investigation and critical thinking.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows the inquiry developed in response to evidence, demonstrating genuine investigation and critical thinking. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a claim and evidence.
items.answer: A claim is a statement a source asserts; evidence is the data or observation that supports or challenges it.
items.markingKey: A claim is a statement a source asserts; evidence is the data or observation that supports or challenges it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between analysis and description.
items.answer: Description says what the system does; analysis explains how and why it affects people and what the implications are.
items.markingKey: Description says what the system does; analysis explains how and why it affects people and what the implications are. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a topic and an inquiry focus.
items.answer: A topic is a broad area (e.g. social media); an inquiry focus names a specific system and its impacts on specific people (e.g. TikTok's recommendation system and the body image of teenagers at my school).
items.markingKey: A topic is a broad area (e.g. social media); an inquiry focus names a specific system and its impacts on specific people (e.g. TikTok's recommendation system and the body image of teenagers at my school). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "The process document should repeat the content of the presentation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It explains how the inquiry was carried out and developed, not its findings.
items.markingKey: It explains how the inquiry was carried out and developed, not its findings. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between limitation of a source and value of a source.
items.answer: Value is what makes the source useful (expertise, first-hand access); limitation is what restricts its usefulness (bias, small sample, age).
items.markingKey: Value is what makes the source useful (expertise, first-hand access); limitation is what restricts its usefulness (bias, small sample, age). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: the digital system and focus: 1 min 30 s; evidence from sources: 2 min 30 s; impacts and implications for stakeholders: 4 min 30 s; conclusion and further inquiry: 1 min 30 s

items.stem: Using a local delivery-app inquiry as an example, explain choosing a real-world system.
items.answer: A student investigates how a food-delivery platform's algorithmic management affects riders in their city, using interviews, the company's policies and news reports. Local relevance gives access to primary evidence and multiple perspectives.
items.markingKey: Context (A student investigates how a food-delivery platform's algorithmic management affects riders in their city, using interviews, the company's policies and news reports.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: local relevance gives access to primary evidence and multiple perspectives. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to choosing a real-world system.

items.stem: Briefly describe a process-document entry and explain what it reveals about documenting development of the inquiry.
items.answer: A student explains that their original focus on "online gaming" was narrowed to "loot boxes in one popular game and spending by teenagers" after finding UK and Belgian regulatory reports. Concise reflection shows how evidence shaped the focus.
items.markingKey: Context (A student explains that their original focus on "online gaming" was narrowed to "loot boxes in one popular game and spending by teenagers" after finding UK and Belgian regulatory reports.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: concise reflection shows how evidence shaped the focus. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to documenting development of the inquiry.

items.stem: For their inquiry, a student sends a questionnaire to 200 students; 80 reply. Of these, 42 say they have seen a deepfake video. Calculate the response rate and the percentage of respondents who have seen a deepfake video. Explain one limitation of this evidence and how the student could address it.
items.answer: response rate 40%; 52.5% of respondents; small, self-selected sample may not be representative; corroborate with interviews, published studies or wider data, and acknowledge the limitation

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Primary sources are more valuable than secondary sources for the inquiry project."
items.answer: Combining primary and secondary sources gives the most balanced and reliable inquiry.
